 Election Day 2026: Live updates
 Updates from around the state as Virginians select their next slate of congressional representatives and votes on three constitutional amendments.

 Virginians approve reproductive rights constitutional amendment, enshrine access to abortions
 By Charlotte Rene Woods - Tuesday November 3, 2026 10:04 pm 
 Chrisi West smiles shortly after the Virginians For Reproductive Victory campaign declares victory on a ballot referendum to enshrine reproductive rights into the state’s constitution. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury) 
 By 10 p.m. Tuesday, more than 61% of Virginia voters approved enshrining reproductive rights into the state’s constitution, opting to permanently protect contraception, fertility treatments and abortion access.  
 The amendment was one of the most contentious issues of the 2026 campaign cycle, with lawmakers, healthcare professionals, advocates and the public at odds over the measure. The Associated Press declared that it had been approved by a majority of voters at 9:01 p.m. 
 Virginians for Reproductive Freedom, the leading group advocating for the amendment’s passage, celebrated the outcome Tuesday evening in Richmond.  
 “Never again will our reproductive rights be a political football in Virginia,” said Han Jones, campaign manager for VFR, the coalition of advocacy organizations that spearheaded outreach about the amendment. 
 “It takes multi-year concerted work, but as you can see in Virginia, it’s paying off,” Jones added at a victory party organized by the group in Richmond. Supporters celebrated the news with shouts of joy and dancing.  
 The amendment passed the General Assembly for two years in a row to qualify for the ballot. Proponents had sought the measure because Virginia is the only southern state without deep restrictions or bans on abortion.  
 The amendments cements Virginians’ right to obtain birth control medication or devices, as well as fertility treatments.  
 It makes access to abortions guaranteed for any reason through their second trimester and a single physician — instead of three, as in previous years — will need to approve late-term abortions.  
 Ballot Question 1 is part of a trio of constitutional amendments voters decided on Election Day.  
 The other two would remove a ban on same-sex marriage in Virginia and automatically restore voting rights to formerly incarcerated felons who have completed their sentences.  
 Check back here later for our full report on the amendments. 
 Virginia precincts experienced threats, ran out of ballots, elections chief says
 By Samantha Willis - 9:00 pm 
 (Chart courtesy The Virginia Department of Elections) 
 Two shooting threats and a bomb threat were reported at precincts in the City of Richmond on Election Day, Virginia Elections Commissioner Steve Kioski said in a Tuesday night press briefing, with police investigating shooting threats at a middle school and high school. 
 Richmond Police “found no suspicious activity or evidence of an immediate threat at the locations assessed,” the department said in a statement . The phoned-in threats occurred at Thomas Jefferson High school Tuesday at 12:42 p.m., with another called into Barack Obama Elementary School just under an hour later.  
 The incidents did not interrupt voting, Koski said.  
 Two precincts in Nottoway County temporarily ran out of ballots, triggering a delay of up to two hours for some voters. The Nottoway circuit court denied a petition to extend the voting hours at the precincts, the commission stated. 
 “We did receive some reports that some voters may have not stayed to wait, so I can’t say if some of these voters returned later to vote,” Koski said.  
 Koski also gave a detailed overview of how the election results would be tabulated and certified, a step scheduled to take place Dec. 7. Dec. 17 is the deadline for eligible recount petitions to be filed. The margin of victory must be less than 1% to be eligible for a recount. 
 Warner wins fourth term representing Virginia in U.S. Senate
 By Samantha Willis - 7:28 pm 
 U.S. Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) speaking at a press conference Oct. 14 in support of federal workers. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters) 
 Democrat incumbent Mark Warner is the projected winner of the race for Virginia’s U.S. Senate seat, defeating Republican challenger Bert Mizusawa. The Associated Press declared the three-term senator the winner at 7 p.m., just as polls closed statewide.  
 Though no votes had yet been reported by the Department of Elections, the AP said the contest was one that was “not expected to be competitive when all available evidence points to an overwhelming victory.”  
 That evidence could include past vote results, pre-election polling, campaign fundraising and spending and results from AP’s Voter Poll voter survey. 
 Warner finished the race with a fundraising total of $27,493,348 , according to the Virginia Public Access Project, while Mizusawa raised $1,097,119 . 
 Warner was first elected to represent Virginia in the U.S. Senate in 2008 and vice chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee. He was governor from 2002 to 2006 and failed his first attempt at a Senate run in 1996. This year, he pledged that if he was elected, it would be his final term. 
 Check back later to read The Mercury’s full coverage of the election results.   
 Back in the studio: The Mercury’s Markus Schmidt returns to WWBT’s election night panel at 8 p.m.
 By Staff Report - 7:00 pm 
 Election night means a homecoming of sorts for The Mercury’s Markus Schmidt , who returns to WWBT’s panel Tuesday for another year of live analysis as Virginia’s results roll in.
 The Mercury’s senior politics reporter and deputy editor will join 12 On Your Side’s Rachel DePompa and Jasmine Turner, along with University of Richmond political scientist Ernest McGowen, to break down the races, turnout and what the returns reveal about Virginia’s political direction.
 Coverage airs from 8 to 10 p.m. on WWBT 12 On Your Side .
 Schmidt is pictured with fellow panelists during the station’s coverage of the 2024 presidential election.

 Spotsylvania voters flock to polls in pivotal election
 By Nathaniel Cline - 4:41 pm 
 A view from inside a voting precinct in Spotsylvania County on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury) 
 Spotsylvania voters Eric and Cathy Sunshine said their families, including their grandchildren, motivated them to vote at Spotsylvania County’s Fire Rescue 7 Station on Tuesday. 
 The couple, representing 4,922 eligible voters at the 7th Congressional District precinct, said addressing issues like high living costs starts with voting for who represents them in Congress in one of Virginia’s most competitive districts. 
 “We have to consider what their future is going to look like,” Cathy Sunshine said. “We’ll be gone, but they’ll have to live with what’s happening.” 
 In the 7th District race , Democratic incumbent Eugene Vindman is seeking a second term against challengers including Republican Douglas Ollivant and four independent candidates. 
 On Tuesday, precinct officials said it’s been “busy,” with a steady flow of voters and just over 1,100 check-ins by 3 p.m. The precinct has 4,922 voters. 
 Eric Sunshine, one of those in-person voters, named family as his chief motivation to vote, saying that the country can’t have a “dictatorship” in America under President Donald Trump. 
 “We’ve had enough of that,” Eric Sunshine said. “We need a president who follows the rules, just like the rest of us are expected to.” 
 Voters Mary Byrnes and Sherry Rodriguez said voting on Virginia’s constitutional amendments was a priority for them 
 “I feel like it’s important to be present, especially in the current political climate, and to recognize that every vote really does matter right now,” Byrnes said. 
 Rodriguez said she voted to “maintain our liberties, protect our freedoms, and preserve what makes America great.” 
 “We want to keep it going and walk away from all this nonsense that’s going on,” she said. “We were brought up with these traditions, and let’s keep it that way.” 
 Last updated: 4:42 pm
 DOJ monitors admitted at polls in two Virginia localities; ballot printing problems reported
 By Markus Schmidt - 4:18 pm 
 Virginia Elections Commissioner Steve Koski gave a mid-day briefing to press on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury) 
 Federal election monitors were allowed inside polling places in Charlottesville and Fairfax County on Tuesday, but officials in Prince William County and Virginia Beach denied them access, Virginia Elections Commissioner Steve Koski said during an afternoon media briefing.
 “We have not heard of any issues related to them,” Koski said, referring to the observers.
 The U.S. Department of Justice on Tuesday morning announced plans to monitor those four jurisdictions as part of a nationwide deployment of approximately 1,000 monitors and observers across all 50 states.
 Koski said DOJ monitors must obtain permission from local officials to observe inside polling places. Charlottesville and Fairfax granted access, while monitors in Prince William and Virginia Beach remained outside the 40-foot restricted area surrounding polling place entrances.
 The two localities “decided to not permit them in as neutral observers in the polling location,” he said.
 Koski also reported ballot printing problems in Carroll County, Waynesboro and Harrisonburg. Some ballots could not be scanned by voting machines, although the information printed on them was correct.
 “There was nothing wrong with the content on the ballot. It was just its inability to be read by the machine,” Koski said.
 Waynesboro and Harrisonburg used ballot-on-demand printers, allowing voting to continue without disruption, he said. Carroll County received newly printed replacement ballots. Ballots already cast that could not be scanned were secured for later counting.
 “They will be counted,” Koski said.
 The commissioner also released updated early voting figures showing a sharp increase from the previous midterm election.
 Virginia recorded 1,647,097 early votes, including returned mailed absentee ballots, compared with 992,227 in 2022. Of this year’s total, 1,319,091 ballots were cast early in person, up from 681,561 four years ago.
 The state has 6,494,236 registered voters, Koski said.
 “So again, we’ve seen just a lot of interest this year in early voting,” he said.
 Virginians are voting for a U.S. senator and all 11 members of the state’s U.S. House delegation, along with three constitutional amendments and various local contests and referendums.
 Koski urged voters to check both sides of their ballots and reminded them that anyone in line by 7 p.m. can still vote.
 Eligible residents who have not registered may do so at the polling place assigned to their residential address and cast a provisional ballot.
 Voters with completed absentee ballots should return them in person by 7 p.m. if possible, Koski said. Those mailing their ballots Tuesday should ask postal workers for a hand-stamped postmark.
 Last updated: 4:31 pm
 In Caroline County, 7th District voters say ‘yes’ to constitutional amendments
 By Samantha Willis - 3:29 pm 
 Melissa Correa, left, with her mother, Sarah Seabrooks, outside the West Mattaponi precinct in Caroline County on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Samantha Willis/Virginia Mercury) 
 Melissa Correa voted for the first time at the West Mattaponi precinct inside Caroline High School in a rural swath of Virginia’s 7th Congressional District .
 “Every vote matters. I want to see change,” Correa, who was joined by her mother, Sarah Seabrooks, said. They were among the over 330 voters election workers said had passed through the precinct by 3:15 p.m.
 The women chose between Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman, who is vying for a second term, Republican Douglas Ollivant and four independent candidates. They said they supported the passage of all three constitutional amendments to permanently protext reproductive rights, same-sex marriage and voting restoration for former felons.
 “I do believe in everybody being equal, including same-sex couples,” Seabrooks said. “And people who committed felonies, if they paid their debt to society, they should be able to vote.”
 “It’s their body,” Correa said of the reproductive rights amendment that would preserve access to contraception, assistive family planning tools like in vitro fertilization and abortion.
 “Some of the abortion laws are so stringent that people have died when they needed one, because doctors are afraid to give them one,” Seabrooks said.
 The country is not progressing and would fare better under new leadership, both said, adding that voting puts civil rights into action.
 “If you don’t vote, you don’t have a right to complain,” Seabrooks stated.
 Richmond schools superintendent ‘hopeful’ voters will adopt 1% sales tax option
 By Charlotte Rene Woods - 3:10 pm 
 City of Richmond Public Schools Superintendent Jason Kamras visited Museum District polling locations Tuesday afternoon, mingling with voters and stumping for a local referendum that could allow the locality to impose a 1% sales tax to fund school infrastructure improvements. 
 Decked out in a t-shirt advertising the referendum and armed with a handful of flyers, Kamras explained that he’s been waiting a “long time” to see the proposal on local ballots. 
 The ballot question asks if the vicinity should levy the additional sales tax of up to 1%, an option that was only available to eight localities statewide before state law changed this year.  
 If approved by voters, Richmond’s sales tax would jump from 6% to 7% — which could generate an estimated $50 million annually. That money could only be used for new school construction or renovation. 
 A state report found that more than half of Virginia ’s public schools are more than 50 years old, with several in a state of disrepair. 
 “I’m hopeful that the city of Richmond comes through, and this will be life changing for our kids,” Kamras, who has led the district since 2018, said. 
 Steady voting in Chesterfield as amendments draw questions
 By Markus Schmidt - 1:53 pm 
 Voting at Meadowdale Library in Chesterfield County on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury) 
 Voting was steady at two Chesterfield County precincts Tuesday morning, while lines formed at Stonebridge Recreation Center in the early afternoon as residents cast ballots in congressional races and weighed three constitutional amendments and a proposed 1% sales tax for school construction.
 At Meadowdale Library, precinct chief Jane Wynn said 187 voters had cast ballots by 11:30 a.m. “It’s moving,” she said.
 At Falling Creek Middle School, precinct chief Bob Ewing reported about 300 voters by noon, with no unusual activity. He said heavy early voting appeared to have reduced Election Day traffic.
 Neither precinct chief reported seeing federal election monitors. Chesterfield was not among the four Virginiajurisdictions the U.S. Department of Justice identified for monitoring, which included Charlottesville, Fairfax, Prince William and Virginia Beach.
 Outside Meadowdale Library, Dale District Supervisor LeQuan Hylton, a candidate in Tuesday’s special election in the district, spoke with voters about the amendments and school funding referendum.
 “My job is to just let people know what the amendments mean and how they can contribute to people’s lives,” Hylton said.
 He supports the proposals to protect reproductive rights, guarantee marriage equality and automatically restore voting rights upon release from incarceration following a felony conviction.
 Hylton also encouraged voters to back the school construction tax, saying it would help provide a safe community with strong schools.
 Chesterfield County Supervisor LeQuan Hylton outside Meadowdale Library on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury) 
 Democratic volunteer Jeanne Pauley, who distributed sample ballots outside the library, said voters were friendly and turnout had been steady.
 “And we had a whole lot of early voters earlier, but people are friendly and happy to be voting, and that’s great,” she said. Ewing, who also worked during early voting, said some voters had questions about the constitutional amendments.
 “Some people wondered and asked for clarifications and explanations of what the amendments were, or a specific word in an amendment,” he said.
 At Stonebridge Recreation Center, Democratic volunteer Lisa Dewey said she encountered similar questions during her early voting shifts. Some voters already planned to support the amendments but wanted to better understand their wording.
 “There were several times where I’d explain it to them, show them the language, and it confirmed what they wanted to do, but it gave them a little bit of extra information,” Dewey said.
 In the 1st Congressional District’s New Kent County, poll chiefs note increase in voters
 By Shannon Heckt - 1:20 pm 
 A woman votes at Hopewell Baptist Church in New Kent, where Precinct Chief Wesley Taylor said that nearly 300 voters had come through by noon on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury) 
 During the lunch hour on Election Day, a steady stream of voters trickled through a New Kent County precinct in Virginia’s 1st Congressional District .   
 Democrat Shannon Taylor is trying to unseat the Republican incumbent U.S. Rob Wittman, with his supporters campaigning  at multiple polling sites in the county Tuesday. 
 “A big part of the Virginia economy is military related. So very happy to see the work he has already done and I feel like we need to support that to continue on,” said Laura Ecimovic, a member of the New Kent Republican Party. 
 At the Hopewell Baptist Church polling site precinct, Chief Wesley Taylor said that there had been 285 voters by noon, which he said is more than normal for a midterm election. Over the last 15 years, he said that more and more people are turning out to vote there on average. 
 Along New Kent’s winding, -lined roads, an equal split of Wittman and Shannon Taylor signs dotted front yards. A group of Taylor supporters camped out at George W. Watkins Elementary School, includingVictoria Waldron with the New Kent Dems. 
 Waldron said that  the national focus on VA-01 and the potential for a close race shows how more voters are getting involved. 
 “I think people’s awareness of the money in politics and what we can’t afford (is increasing). What is Rob Wittman doing for us?” she said 
 Watkins Elementary is one of the busiest voting precincts in the county, according to Chief Danielle Davis. By noon, 614 voters had cast ballots there, with more filtering in all afternoon  
 Davis said she expects a surge of voters to come in after they get off work. 
 Constitutional amendments would ensure Virginia is ‘a safe place,’ Stafford voter says
 By Nathaniel Cline - 12:15 pm 
 A view from inside a voting precinct in Stafford County on Nov. 3, 2026. The polling place is in Virginia’s 7th Congressional District. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury) 
 Stafford County voters at Hartwood Elementary School recorded the highest in-person turnout four years ago, with over 2,015 voters. By late morning on Tuesday, the polling place was on track to reach that milestone again. 
 As of 11:45 a.m., the precinct was averaging about 120 voters an hour. 
 A total of 851 voters had checked in, representing 16% of the 5,000 voters registered in the Hartwood Precinct. 
 As in previous years, voters are deciding the winner of the 7th Congressional District race . Democratic incumbent Eugene Vindman faces Republican Douglas Ollivant, and Libertarian Taner Lopez. Independents  Alaha Ahrar, Randall Terry and Joshua Ertle are also on the ballot. 
 Charles Lawrence, a Stafford County voter, said voting was important for him today because he wanted to do his part to keep Republicans in control. 
 “I just want the Republicans to win because I don’t want everything to be overturned over what was done the last two years,” said Lawrence. “I want things to keep going the way they’re going and I would like to get the (Iran) war over also, so hopefully they will.” 
 Stafford voter Kenya Bell said casting her ballot on the constitutional amendments to protect reproductive rights, marriage equality and voting restoration for former felons was a priority for her. 
 Without the choice to approve the amendments, she said would’ve had to move out of the commonwealth. 
 “There was too much on the line,” Bell said. “In this current environment and this current culture, (opponents) are looking to strip away and gut out all of our rights federally. So I needed to make sure that Virginia was going to be a safe place to continue to reside.” 
 Some voters cited  critical concerns including  mounting economic pressures, federal employment shifts, a lack of affordable housing, and infrastructure needs. 
 The 7th District seat is one of the most competitive in Virginia. 
 Jones urges Virginians to vote, thanks election workers
 By Markus Schmidt - 10:01 am 
 Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones in Hampton, Va., August 2026.  (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury) 
 Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones encouraged eligible voters to cast their ballots Tuesday and thanked election officials for their work as polls opened across the state.
 “Our ability to choose our leaders with free, fair, and safe elections is what makes our republic special,” Jones said in an Election Day statement.
 Jones urged Virginians who had not yet voted to visit their polling place or return their absentee ballot.
 “I also want to thank the dedicated election officials who are working long hours today and will be working well into the early morning hours in support of our democratic process,” he said.
 Last updated: 10:01 am
 DOJ lists four Virginia jurisdictions for Election Day monitoring
 By Markus Schmidt - 9:20 am 
 The U.S. Department of Justice plans to send election monitors or observers to Charlottesville, Fairfax, Prince William and Virginia Beach on Tuesday as part of what it calls its largest election monitoring effort.
 The department announced approximately 1,000 monitors and observers nationwide, with deployments in all 50 states for the first time. The release did not specify polling locations or how many personnel would be assigned to Virginia.
 Coordinated by the department’s Civil Rights Division, the effort will check compliance with federal voting rights laws, including protections against voter intimidation and discrimination and requirements ensuring access for voters with disabilities.
 “I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said in the announcement.
 Virginia Elections Commissioner Steve Koski, appointed by Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger, told The Mercury in a recent interview that state and local officials had prepared for potential disruptions.
 “I cannot speak for any potential actions that anybody else would take. But regardless, I feel prepared, I feel our localities are prepared to run this election well, and we will do so in accordance with the law,” he said.
 Voters can report concerns about federal voting rights violations to the department at 1-800-253-3931 , by email at [email protected] or through its civil rights complaint portal .
 Last updated: 9:21 am
 Spanberger urges Virginians to vote, citing ‘chaos out of Washington’
 By Markus Schmidt - 8:25 am 
 Gov. Abigail Spanberger speaks to reporters in Richmond, July 2026. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury) 
 Gov. Abigail Spanberger urged eligible Virginians to vote Tuesday, pointing to congressional races and three proposed constitutional amendments as opportunities to shape the state’s and country’s future.
 “Virginians can use their votes to choose representatives who they believe will address their top-of-mind challenges, contend with the chaos out of Washington, and always put them first,” Spanberger said in an Election Day statement.
 The Democratic governor also highlighted amendments addressing reproductive rights, marriage equality and voting rights.
 “At a time when chaos and uncertainty continue to dominate our national politics, we can send a clear message about the future we want to build — one grounded in accountability, steady leadership, and a commitment to delivering for people.”
 Last updated: 8:47 am
 Polls are open, Virginia
 By Staff Report - 8:23 am 
 Virginians will vote Tuesday in the 2026 midterm elections, with control of Congress and three proposed constitutional amendments at stake after a record early voting turnout.
 Polls are open statewide from 6 a.m. until 7 p.m., giving voters their final opportunity to weigh in on races for the U.S. Senate and all 11 of Virginia’s U.S. House seats, along with proposed protections for reproductive rights, marriage equality and voting rights.
 Read this to get prepared before you vote, and check out our voter guide if you need to learn more about the candidates, races and amendments on the ballot.
 We’ll be posting updates from around the state all day; check back here soon.

 const getRelativeTime = (current, target) => {
 const timeDiff = Math.floor((target - current) / 1000);
 const relativeTime = new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('en', {
 numeric: 'always',
 });
 if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60) { // Within minute
 return relativeTime.format(Math.min(Math.round(timeDiff), 1), 'second');
 } else if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60 * 60) { // Within hour
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / 60), 'minute');
 } else if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60 * 60 * 24) { // Within day
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / (60 * 60)), 'hour');
 } else if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60 * 60 * 24 * 7) { // Within week
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / (60 * 60 * 24)), 'day');
 } else if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60 * 60 * 24 * 30) { // Within month
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / ( 60 * 60 * 24 * 7)), 'week');
 } else if (Math.abs(timeDiff) < 60 * 60 * 24 * 365) { // Within year
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / ( 60 * 60 * 24 * 30)), 'month');
 } else { // Year+
 return relativeTime.format(Math.round(timeDiff / (60 * 60 * 24 * 365)), 'year');
 }
 }

 Democrat incumbent Mark Warner is the projected winner of the race for Virginia’s U.S. Senate seat, defeating Republican challenger Bert Mizusawa. The Associated Press declared the three-term senator the winner at 7 p.m., just as polls closed statewide. 
 Though no votes had yet been reported by the Department of Elections, the AP said the contest was one that was “not expected to be competitive when all available evidence points to an overwhelming victory.” 
 That evidence could include past vote results, pre-election polling, campaign fundraising and spending and results from AP’s Voter Poll voter survey.
 Warner finished the race with a fundraising total of $27,493,348 , according to the Virginia Public Access Project, while Mizusawa raised $1,097,119 .
 Warner was first elected to represent Virginia in the U.S. Senate in 2008 and vice chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee. He was governor from 2002 to 2006 and failed his first attempt at a Senate run in 1996. This year, he pledged that if he was elected, it would be his final term.
 Check back later to read The Mercury’s full coverage of the election results.

 Spotsylvania voters flock to polls in pivotal election
 By Nathaniel Cline - 4:41 pm
 Spotsylvania voters Eric and Cathy Sunshine said their families, including their grandchildren, motivated them to vote at Spotsylvania County’s Fire Rescue 7 Station on Tuesday.
 The couple, representing 4,922 eligible voters at the 7th Congressional District precinct, said addressing issues like high living costs starts with voting for who represents them in Congress in one of Virginia’s most competitive districts.
 “We have to consider what their future is going to look like,” Cathy Sunshine said. “We’ll be gone, but they’ll have to live with what’s happening.”
 In the 7th District race , Democratic incumbent Eugene Vindman is seeking a second term against challengers including Republican Douglas Ollivant and four independent candidates.
 On Tuesday, precinct officials said it’s been “busy,” with a steady flow of voters and just over 1,100 check-ins by 3 p.m. The precinct has 4,922 voters.
 Eric Sunshine, one of those in-person voters, named family as his chief motivation to vote, saying that the country can’t have a “dictatorship” in America under President Donald Trump.
 “We’ve had enough of that,” Eric Sunshine said. “We need a president who follows the rules, just like the rest of us are expected to.”
 Voters Mary Byrnes and Sherry Rodriguez said voting on Virginia’s constitutional amendments was a priority for them
 “I feel like it’s important to be present, especially in the current political climate, and to recognize that every vote really does matter right now,” Byrnes said.
 Rodriguez said she voted to “maintain our liberties, protect our freedoms, and preserve what makes America great.”
 “We want to keep it going and walk away from all this nonsense that’s going on,” she said. “We were brought up with these traditions, and let’s keep it that way.”

 DOJ monitors admitted at polls in two Virginia localities; ballot printing problems reported
 By Markus Schmidt - 4:18 pm
 Federal election monitors were allowed inside polling places in Charlottesville and Fairfax County on Tuesday, but officials in Prince William County and Virginia Beach denied them access, Virginia Elections Commissioner Steve Koski said during an afternoon media briefing.
 “We have not heard of any issues related to them,” Koski said, referring to the observers.
 The U.S. Department of Justice on Tuesday morning announced plans to monitor those four jurisdictions as part of a nationwide deployment of approximately 1,000 monitors and observers across all 50 states.
 Koski said DOJ monitors must obtain permission from local officials to observe inside polling places. Charlottesville and Fairfax granted access, while monitors in Prince William and Virginia Beach remained outside the 40-foot restricted area surrounding polling place entrances.
 The two localities “decided to not permit them in as neutral observers in the polling location,” he said.
 Koski also reported ballot printing problems in Carroll County, Waynesboro and Harrisonburg. Some ballots could not be scanned by voting machines, although the information printed on them was correct.
 “There was nothing wrong with the content on the ballot. It was just its inability to be read by the machine,” Koski said.
 Waynesboro and Harrisonburg used ballot-on-demand printers, allowing voting to continue without disruption, he said. Carroll County received newly printed replacement ballots. Ballots already cast that could not be scanned were secured for later counting.
 “They will be counted,” Koski said.
 The commissioner also released updated early voting figures showing a sharp increase from the previous midterm election.
 Virginia recorded 1,647,097 early votes, including returned mailed absentee ballots, compared with 992,227 in 2022. Of this year’s total, 1,319,091 ballots were cast early in person, up from 681,561 four years ago.
 The state has 6,494,236 registered voters, Koski said.
 “So again, we’ve seen just a lot of interest this year in early voting,” he said.
 Virginians are voting for a U.S. senator and all 11 members of the state’s U.S. House delegation, along with three constitutional amendments and various local contests and referendums.
 Koski urged voters to check both sides of their ballots and reminded them that anyone in line by 7 p.m. can still vote.
 Eligible residents who have not registered may do so at the polling place assigned to their residential address and cast a provisional ballot.
 Voters with completed absentee ballots should return them in person by 7 p.m. if possible, Koski said. Those mailing their ballots Tuesday should ask postal workers for a hand-stamped postmark.

 In Caroline County, 7th District voters say ‘yes’ to constitutional amendments
 By Samantha Willis - 3:29 pm
 Melissa Correa voted for the first time at the West Mattaponi precinct inside Caroline High School in a rural swath of Virginia’s 7th Congressional District .
 “Every vote matters. I want to see change,” Correa, who was joined by her mother, Sarah Seabrooks, said. They were among the over 330 voters election workers said had passed through the precinct by 3:15 p.m.
 The women chose between Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. Eugene Vindman, who is vying for a second term, Republican Douglas Ollivant and four independent candidates. They said they supported the passage of all three constitutional amendments to permanently protext reproductive rights, same-sex marriage and voting restoration for former felons.
 “I do believe in everybody being equal, including same-sex couples,” Seabrooks said. “And people who committed felonies, if they paid their debt to society, they should be able to vote.”
 “It’s their body,” Correa said of the reproductive rights amendment that would preserve access to contraception, assistive family planning tools like in vitro fertilization and abortion.
 “Some of the abortion laws are so stringent that people have died when they needed one, because doctors are afraid to give them one,” Seabrooks said.
 The country is not progressing and would fare better under new leadership, both said, adding that voting puts civil rights into action.
 “If you don’t vote, you don’t have a right to complain,” Seabrooks stated.
 Richmond schools superintendent ‘hopeful’ voters will adopt 1% sales tax option
 By Charlotte Rene Woods - 3:10 pm
 City of Richmond Public Schools Superintendent Jason Kamras visited Museum District polling locations Tuesday afternoon, mingling with voters and stumping for a local referendum that could allow the locality to impose a 1% sales tax to fund school infrastructure improvements.
 Decked out in a t-shirt advertising the referendum and armed with a handful of flyers, Kamras explained that he’s been waiting a “long time” to see the proposal on local ballots.
 The ballot question asks if the vicinity should levy the additional sales tax of up to 1%, an option that was only available to eight localities statewide before state law changed this year. 
 If approved by voters, Richmond’s sales tax would jump from 6% to 7% — which could generate an estimated $50 million annually. That money could only be used for new school construction or renovation.
 A state report found that more than half of Virginia’s public schools are more than 50 years old, with several in a state of disrepair.
 “I’m hopeful that the city of Richmond comes through, and this will be life changing for our kids,” Kamras, who has led the district since 2018, said.
 Steady voting in Chesterfield as amendments draw questions
 By Markus Schmidt - 1:53 pm
 Voting was steady at two Chesterfield County precincts Tuesday morning, while lines formed at Stonebridge Recreation Center in the early afternoon as residents cast ballots in congressional races and weighed three constitutional amendments and a proposed 1% sales tax for school construction.
 At Meadowdale Library, precinct chief Jane Wynn said 187 voters had cast ballots by 11:30 a.m. “It’s moving,” she said.
 At Falling Creek Middle School, precinct chief Bob Ewing reported about 300 voters by noon, with no unusual activity. He said heavy early voting appeared to have reduced Election Day traffic.
 Neither precinct chief reported seeing federal election monitors. Chesterfield was not among the four Virginiajurisdictions the U.S. Department of Justice identified for monitoring, which included Charlottesville, Fairfax, Prince William and Virginia Beach.
 Outside Meadowdale Library, Dale District Supervisor LeQuan Hylton, a candidate in Tuesday’s special election in the district, spoke with voters about the amendments and school funding referendum.
 “My job is to just let people know what the amendments mean and how they can contribute to people’s lives,” Hylton said.
 He supports the proposals to protect reproductive rights, guarantee marriage equality and automatically restore voting rights upon release from incarceration following a felony conviction.
 Hylton also encouraged voters to back the school construction tax, saying it would help provide a safe community with strong schools.
 Democratic volunteer Jeanne Pauley, who distributed sample ballots outside the library, said voters were friendly and turnout had been steady.
 “And we had a whole lot of early voters earlier, but people are friendly and happy to be voting, and that’s great,” she said.
Ewing, who also worked during early voting, said some voters had questions about the constitutional amendments.
 “Some people wondered and asked for clarifications and explanations of what the amendments were, or a specific word in an amendment,” he said.
 At Stonebridge Recreation Center, Democratic volunteer Lisa Dewey said she encountered similar questions during her early voting shifts. Some voters already planned to support the amendments but wanted to better understand their wording.
 “There were several times where I’d explain it to them, show them the language, and it confirmed what they wanted to do, but it gave them a little bit of extra information,” Dewey said.
 In the 1st Congressional District’s New Kent County, poll chiefs note increase in voters
 By Shannon Heckt - 1:20 pm
 During the lunch hour on Election Day, a steady stream of voters trickled through a New Kent County precinct in Virginia’s 1st Congressional District .  
 Democrat Shannon Taylor is trying to unseat the Republican incumbent U.S. Rob Wittman, with his supporters campaigning  at multiple polling sites in the county Tuesday.
 “A big part of the Virginia economy is military related. So very happy to see the work he has already done and I feel like we need to support that to continue on,” said Laura Ecimovic, a member of the New Kent Republican Party.
 At the Hopewell Baptist Church polling site precinct, Chief Wesley Taylor said that there had been 285 voters by noon, which he said is more than normal for a midterm election. Over the last 15 years, he said that more and more people are turning out to vote there on average.
 Along New Kent’s winding, -lined roads, an equal split of Wittman and Shannon Taylor signs dotted front yards. A group of Taylor supporters camped out at George W. Watkins Elementary School, includingVictoria Waldron with the New Kent Dems.
 Waldron said that  the national focus on VA-01 and the potential for a close race shows how more voters are getting involved.
 “I think people’s awareness of the money in politics and what we can’t afford (is increasing). What is Rob Wittman doing for us?” she said
 Watkins Elementary is one of the busiest voting precincts in the county, according to Chief Danielle Davis. By noon, 614 voters had cast ballots there, with more filtering in all afternoon 
 Davis said she expects a surge of voters to come in after they get off work.
 Constitutional amendments would ensure Virginia is ‘a safe place,’ Stafford voter says
 By Nathaniel Cline - 12:15 pm
 Stafford County voters at Hartwood Elementary School recorded the highest in-person turnout four years ago, with over 2,015 voters. By late morning on Tuesday, the polling place was on track to reach that milestone again.
 As of 11:45 a.m., the precinct was averaging about 120 voters an hour.
 A total of 851 voters had checked in, representing 16% of the 5,000 voters registered in the Hartwood Precinct.
 As in previous years, voters are deciding the winner of the 7th Congressional District race . Democratic incumbent Eugene Vindman faces Republican Douglas Ollivant, and Libertarian Taner Lopez. Independents  Alaha Ahrar, Randall Terry and Joshua Ertle are also on the ballot.
 Charles Lawrence, a Stafford County voter, said voting was important for him today because he wanted to do his part to keep Republicans in control.
 “I just want the Republicans to win because I don’t want everything to be overturned over what was done the last two years,” said Lawrence. “I want things to keep going the way they’re going and I would like to get the (Iran) war over also, so hopefully they will.”
 Stafford voter Kenya Bell said casting her ballot on the constitutional amendments to protect reproductive rights, marriage equality and voting restoration for former felons was a priority for her.
 Without the choice to approve the amendments, she said would’ve had to move out of the commonwealth.
 “There was too much on the line,” Bell said. “In this current environment and this current culture, (opponents) are looking to strip away and gut out all of our rights federally. So I needed to make sure that Virginia was going to be a safe place to continue to reside.”
 Some voters cited  critical concerns including  mounting economic pressures, federal employment shifts, a lack of affordable housing, and infrastructure needs.
 The 7th District seat is one of the most competitive in Virginia.
 Jones urges Virginians to vote, thanks election workers
 By Markus Schmidt - 10:01 am
 Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones encouraged eligible voters to cast their ballots Tuesday and thanked election officials for their work as polls opened across the state.
 “Our ability to choose our leaders with free, fair, and safe elections is what makes our republic special,” Jones said in an Election Day statement.

 DOJ lists four Virginia jurisdictions for Election Day monitoring
 By Markus Schmidt - 9:20 am
 The U.S. Department of Justice plans to send election monitors or observers to Charlottesville, Fairfax, Prince William and Virginia Beach on Tuesday as part of what it calls its largest election monitoring effort.
 The department announced approximately 1,000 monitors and observers nationwide, with deployments in all 50 states for the first time. The release did not specify polling locations or how many personnel would be assigned to Virginia.
 Coordinated by the department’s Civil Rights Division, the effort will check compliance with federal voting rights laws, including protections against voter intimidation and discrimination and requirements ensuring access for voters with disabilities.
 “I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said in the announcement.
 Virginia Elections Commissioner Steve Koski, appointed by Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger, told The Mercury in a recent interview that state and local officials had prepared for potential disruptions.
 “I cannot speak for any potential actions that anybody else would take. But regardless, I feel prepared, I feel our localities are prepared to run this election well, and we will do so in accordance with the law,” he said.
 Voters can report concerns about federal voting rights violations to the department at 1-800-253-3931 , by email at VEM@usdoj.gov or through its civil rights complaint portal .

 Spanberger urges Virginians to vote, citing ‘chaos out of Washington’
 By Markus Schmidt - 8:25 am
 Gov. Abigail Spanberger urged eligible Virginians to vote Tuesday, pointing to congressional races and three proposed constitutional amendments as opportunities to shape the state’s and country’s future.
 “Virginians can use their votes to choose representatives who they believe will address their top-of-mind challenges, contend with the chaos out of Washington, and always put them first,” Spanberger said in an Election Day statement.
 The Democratic governor also highlighted amendments addressing reproductive rights, marriage equality and voting rights.
